questions.question: A media company uploads source images to S3. The images must be instantly retrievable for 60 days after upload; after that, retrieval within a few hours is acceptable. Archival cost matters. Which lifecycle design fits?
options: Store in Standard, then use a lifecycle rule to transition to Glacier after 60 days
Store in Standard IA, then use a lifecycle rule to expire the objects after 60 days
Store in One-Zone IA, then use a lifecycle rule to transition to Deep Archive after 60 days
Store in Glacier Instant Retrieval and transition to Standard after 60 days
questions.explanation: Standard gives immediate retrieval during the 60-day window and a transition to Glacier at day 60 matches the loosened hours-level retrieval need. Standard IA plus expiration deletes data the company must still keep. One-Zone IA is for easily recreated data, and Deep Archive is normally a later step after a shorter archive tier in this section's designs. Glacier Instant Retrieval is not the right first tier for data needing immediate access at creation.

questions.question: An application on EC2 generates image thumbnails that can be regenerated at any time and only need to be kept for 60 days. Which configuration is most cost-appropriate?
options: Store thumbnails in Standard with a lifecycle rule to transition to Glacier Deep Archive after 60 days
Store thumbnails in One-Zone IA with a lifecycle rule to expire them after 60 days
Store thumbnails in Standard IA with a lifecycle rule to delete noncurrent versions after 60 days
Store thumbnails in Glacier Flexible Retrieval with a lifecycle rule to transition to Standard IA after 60 days
questions.explanation: One-Zone IA suits infrequently accessed data that is easily recreated, and an expiration action deletes it at day 60. Transitioning regenerable thumbnails to Deep Archive keeps charges alive past the 60-day requirement. Noncurrent version deletion only applies to old versions in a versioned bucket, not the current thumbnails. Storing in Glacier and later transitioning back to Standard IA is backwards and keeps data you intended to expire.

questions.question: Objects are infrequently accessed but must still be retrieved quickly when requested, and the data is not easily reproducible. Which storage class is the appropriate lifecycle transition target?
options: Glacier Deep Archive
One-Zone IA
Standard IA
Glacier Flexible Retrieval
questions.explanation: Standard IA is the section's target for infrequently accessed objects that still need fast retrieval. Deep Archive and Glacier Flexible Retrieval are archive tiers for data without fast-access needs. One-Zone IA also serves infrequent access but is chosen for objects that can be easily recreated, which does not match this requirement.

questions.question: A company needs deleted S3 objects recoverable immediately for 30 days and, after that, recoverable within 48 hours for up to 365 days. How should the storage classes be sequenced?
options: Transition current versions to Standard IA at 30 days and expire the bucket at 365 days
Transition noncurrent versions to Glacier Deep Archive at 30 days, then to Standard IA at 365 days
Enable versioning and expire noncurrent versions immediately on deletion
Enable versioning, transition noncurrent versions to Standard IA, then transition them to Glacier Deep Archive
questions.explanation: Versioning keeps deleted objects behind a delete marker, and the noncurrent versions can be moved from Standard IA to Glacier Deep Archive as the 48-hour recovery requirement takes over. Expiring the bucket at 365 days removes objects the rule says must be recoverable. Moving noncurrent versions first to Deep Archive and later to Standard IA reverses the retrieval-time progression. Expiring noncurrent versions immediately destroys the ability to recover deleted objects at all.

questions.question: A versioned bucket's storage cost keeps rising because overwritten objects remain. Which lifecycle action removes them?
options: An expiration action that deletes noncurrent versions
An expiration action that deletes incomplete multipart uploads
A transition action that moves the objects to Standard IA
An expiration action that deletes the current object after 30 days
questions.explanation: Noncurrent version expiration is the action that removes the old versions kept by versioning. Expiring incomplete multipart uploads only cleans up unfinished uploads. A transition to Standard IA changes the storage class of retained versions but does not delete them. Expiring current objects adds delete markers and leaves the underlying versions, and so does not reduce cost.

questions.question: A bucket receives multi-part uploads that applications frequently abandon before completion, and storage charges are growing. What should you add to the lifecycle configuration?
options: A transition of incomplete uploads to One-Zone IA after 7 days
A transition of incomplete uploads to Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days
An expiration action to delete incomplete multipart uploads
An expiration action on noncurrent versions after 7 days
questions.explanation: Expiring incomplete multipart uploads removes the parts that are charged while an upload never completes. Transitioning incomplete uploads assumes partial uploads can be tiered like objects, which does not match the section's cleanup mechanism. Noncurrent version expiration applies only to old object versions in a versioned bucket, which is unrelated to unfinished uploads.

questions.question: Finance department files must follow a lifecycle rule even though teams can upload them under any key path. Other departments' objects must not be affected. Which filter satisfies this?
options: A rule scoped to the prefix s3://mybucket/finance/*
A rule scoped to the object tag Department: Finance
A bucket policy that restricts lifecycle rules to Finance IAM roles
A rule scoped to the prefix s3://mybucket/*, applied to the whole bucket
questions.explanation: Tag-based rules follow the object's metadata regardless of key layout, and only tagged Finance objects match. A prefix rule only works if every Finance object reliably lands under that path, which the requirement rules out. A bucket policy controls access, not lifecycle scope. A whole-bucket rule affects all departments, violating the constraint.

questions.question: A team wants to know which objects are cold and when they should move to Standard IA, but has no data on access patterns yet. What should they do first?
options: Create a lifecycle rule that transitions all objects to Standard IA after 30 days
Enable S3 Storage Class Analysis to collect access patterns and produce reports
Create a lifecycle rule that expires objects after 30 days
Enable versioning so old objects become noncurrent versions
questions.explanation: Storage Class Analysis observes access patterns and produces a daily report that forms the basis for building lifecycle rules. Transitioning everything after 30 days is a guess made without the data the team lacks. Expiring objects does not inform tiering decisions and risks data loss. Versioning retains old versions but says nothing about which objects are cold.

questions.question: Which statement about S3 Storage Class Analysis is correct?
options: It gives recommendations for One-Zone IA and Glacier as well as Standard IA
It performs the storage class transitions automatically once enabled
It takes 24 to 48 hours before analysis appears, and the report is updated daily
It produces recommendations only for Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive
questions.explanation: Analysis takes 24 to 48 hours to begin showing data, and the report refreshes daily. Analysis recommendations cover Standard and Standard IA only and do not work for One-Zone IA or Glacier. Analysis never executes transitions; lifecycle rules do that. Limiting recommendations to Glacier classes misstates which classes are covered.

questions.question: Why should lifecycle configuration include both transition actions and expiration actions rather than choosing one type?
options: Transitions move objects to cheaper classes over time, and expirations delete data that is no longer needed
Transitions delete old versions, and expirations move current objects between storage classes
Expiration actions are required before any transition action can be evaluated
Transitions and expirations can never be combined in a single lifecycle configuration
questions.explanation: Transition actions handle tiering so live objects cost less, while expiration actions remove objects, noncurrent versions and incomplete uploads that no longer need to exist. Deletion belongs to expiration actions, not transitions. No rule requires an expiration before a transition is evaluated. Rules may contain both action types, and one configuration can serve different object sets.
